Fill the Hex Grid

CoordinatesAlgebraLogic
Game: Fill every dot on the board.
How to play: Click any dot to start. After that, each click spins the last filled dot a sixth of a turn around the dot you click, and fills the dot it lands on, unless that one is already filled.

Missteps: 0
Look for the math

Every click here is a small multiplication: two dots go in and a third comes out. With the right clicks you can fill the whole board without a single misstep, on any size, starting anywhere.

A product of two dots

Number the dots by (i, j): i steps along a row and j rows up. When you click P, the last dot L turns 60° clockwise around P, so P, L and the new dot are the corners of an equilateral triangle. In coordinates the new dot is

P * L = (L.i + L.j − P.j, P.i + P.j − L.i)

taken modulo N: a dot that would fall off one edge comes back on the opposite one, as if the board were wrapped round a doughnut. The applet's page words the turn the other way, as the clicked dot turning around the last one; the applet itself turns the last dot around the clicked one, and so does this page. The test checks the 60° clockwise turn with real coordinates.

Why you never get stuck

Hold the last dot L still. Different clicks give different products, so the N² possible clicks reach all N² dots, each exactly once. Whatever is still empty, one click reaches it: solve P * L = T for P. The same holds with P held still, so in the table of all products every row and every column lists each dot once, like a Sudoku. That makes the dots a quasigroup. It is also idempotent, L * L = L, which is why clicking the last dot is always a misstep. The test checked the table for every N from 3 to 40 and filled every board with no missteps.

On the 3 × 3 board, try to fill all nine dots with no missteps. Before each click, picture the equilateral triangle: where must the third corner be?
